headline: FDA knock-back is a setback but not the end of the road — software-based medical devices can revise and resubmit, unlike failed drug trials; valuation at over $1 billion was pricing in approval with no margin for regulatory risk
reasoning: Segal distinguishes between drug and medical device FDA rejections, arguing that a medical device — especially software-based — can adjust its algorithm, narrow scope, or choose a different predicate device and resubmit for 510(k) approval. He notes the company's approval process extended past 250 days versus an initial 150-day first approval, signalling something was awry. He cites Aroa as a precedent on ASX where a 510(k) rejection was eventually overcome. He also flags that a market cap above $1 billion was pricing in approval as a near-certainty, cautioning investors to watch valuation relative to binary regulatory risk.
quote: For a medical device and particularly a medical device that's around software thing, you can change things. So you can either narrow the scope of what you're looking for, you can adjust the algorithm, and you can go back and try and get 510K approval. I think the market at that price point, you know, over $1 billion market cap was probably pricing in that the FDA approval was coming. And I think that just the understanding of the risk factor, that there's no such thing as a certainty, especially because the approval was getting beyond around the 250 day mark when the first approval that they got was only 150 days. So something was awry. Definitely not the end for AQ. I think that they'll be back and be looking to get approval again at some point.
